publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the transfer learning literature - solutions, applications, and the terminology used to describe them
span.quote: This survey paper formally defines transfer learning, presents information on current solutions, and reviews applications applied to transfer learning.

span.label: what to do when the assumption that training and test data share a domain and a distribution does not hold
span.quote: An assumption of traditional machine learning methodologies is the training data and testing data are taken from the same domain, such that the input feature space and data distribution characteristics are the same.

span.label: a formal definition of transfer learning and an explicit account of where the literature's own terms conflict
span.quote: This survey paper formally defines transfer learning, presents information on current solutions, and reviews applications applied to transfer learning.

span.label: critique
span.quote: Throughout the literature on transfer learning, there are a number of terminology inconsistencies. Phrases such as transfer learning and domain adaptation are used to refer to similar processes. The following definitions will be used in this paper.

span.label: improving a target learner using information from a different but related source domain
span.quote: Therefore, there is a need to create high-performance learners trained with more easily obtained data from different domains. This methodology is referred to as transfer learning.

span.label: a survey organised by whether the source and target share a feature space, and by what is transferred
span.term: a survey organised by whether the source and target share a feature space, and by what is transferred
span.quote: The majority of the homogeneous transfer learning solutions employ one of three general strategies which include trying to correct for the marginal distribution difference in the source, trying to correct for the conditional distribution difference in the source, or trying to correct both the marginal and conditional distribution differences in the source.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: WHY TRANSFER LEARNING EXISTS AT ALL: ordinary machine learning assumes train and test come from one domain with one distribution, and the method is what you do when that assumption is false and the target data is expensive to collect
span.quote: An assumption of traditional machine learning methodologies is the training data and testing data are taken from the same domain, such that the input feature space and data distribution characteristics are the same.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: NEGATIVE TRANSFER IS DEFINED BY COMPARISON, NOT BY DAMAGE: a learner trained on the target alone is compared against one trained with the source added, and transfer is negative when the plain learner wins
span.quote: negative transfer occurs when the performance of fT1(·) is greater than the performance of fT2(·). The topic of negative transfer addresses the need to quantify the amount of relatedness between the source domain and the target domain and whether an attempt to transfer knowledge from the source domain should be made.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: PSEUDO LABELS CORRECT A DISTRIBUTION USING GUESSES AT THE THING BEING CORRECTED FOR: with no labeled target data, labels are estimated and then used to fix the conditional distribution - which the paper itself calls problematic
span.quote: To address the lack of labeled target data, some solutions estimate the labels for the target data (called pseudo labels), which are then used to correct the conditional distribution differences. This method is problematic because the conditional distribution corrections are being made with the aid of pseudo labels.

span.label: instance transfer reweights source examples to correct MARGINAL distribution differences, and works best precisely when the CONDITIONAL distribution is already the same
span.quote: A common method used in this case is for instances from the source domain to be reweighted in an attempt to correct for marginal distribution differences.

span.label: the two feature approaches differ in direction: one bends the source onto the target, the other maps both into a shared latent space
span.quote: Feature-based transfer learning approaches are categorized in two ways.

span.label: parameter transfer shares model parameters or combines multiple reweighted source learners into an ensemble for the target
span.quote: The third transfer category is to transfer knowledge through shared parameters of source and target domain learner models or by creating multiple source learner models and optimally combining the reweighted learners (ensemble learners) to form an improved target learner (examples in Gao [37], Bonilla [8], and Evgeniou [33]).

span.label: source classifiers are weighted by how close their conditional distribution is to the target, summed, and used to manufacture pseudo labels for unlabelled target data
span.quote: This is accomplished by first building a classifier for each separate source domain.

span.label: THE FIELD IS DECLARED TERMINOLOGICALLY INCONSISTENT AND THE PAPER SAYS SO IN ITS OWN VOICE: `Throughout the literature on transfer learning, there are A NUMBER OF TERMINOLOGY INCONSISTENCIES. Phrases such as TRANSFER LEARNING and DOMAIN ADAPTATION ARE USED TO REFER TO SIMILAR PROCESSES. THE FOLLOWING DEFINITIONS WILL BE USED IN THIS PAPER.` A survey opening by stipulating the vocabulary because the literature has none.
span.quote: Throughout the literature on transfer learning, there are a number of terminology inconsistencies. Phrases such as transfer learning and domain adaptation are used to refer to similar processes. The following definitions will be used in this paper

span.label: THE SAME CONFIGURATION, RENAMED IN THE NEXT SENTENCE: `In Gong [42] and Blitzer [5], SEMI-SUPERVISED transfer learning is the case of having ABUNDANT LABELED SOURCE DATA AND LIMITED LABELED TARGET DATA.` The sentence immediately before it - quoted separately on this record - gives that exact configuration to Daume and Chattopadhyay as SUPERVISED. The full four-scheme enumeration spans several sentences with a journal running header splicing one of them, so it is carried across four tags on this record rather than asserted from one span.
span.quote: In Gong [42] and Blitzer [5], semi-supervised transfer learning is the case of having abundant labeled source data and limited labeled target data

span.label: AND THE PAPER'S REPAIR IS TO REFUSE THE VOCABULARY ALTOGETHER: `This paper will EXPLICITLY STATE WHEN LABELED AND UNLABELED DATA ARE BEING USED in the source and target domains.` It does not pick a winner and does not coin a fifth term - it describes the configuration and drops the names. THE SAME MOVE CONSORT MADE IN 2010, replacing `intention to treat` with `a more explicit request for information` (schulz2010).
span.quote: This paper will explicitly state when labeled and unlabeled data are being used in the source and target domains

span.label: THE LITERATURE'S VOCABULARY IS INCONSISTENT AND THE PAPER SAYS SO: transfer learning and domain adaptation are used for similar processes, and the supervised / semi-supervised / unsupervised labels mean different things to different authors
span.quote: Throughout the literature on transfer learning, there are a number of terminology inconsistencies. Phrases such as transfer learning and domain adaptation are used to refer to similar processes. The following definitions will be used in this paper.

span.label: Some surveyed solutions are tied to their application and are stated not to generalise to others
span.quote: In some cases, the proposed transfer learning solutions are very specific to the underlying application and cannot be generically used for other applications.

span.label: Correcting the conditional distribution rests on pseudo labels, which the paper names as problematic because the correction uses estimates of the very labels it lacks
span.quote: To address the lack of labeled target data, some solutions estimate the labels for the target data (called pseudo labels), which are then used to correct the conditional distribution differences. This method is problematic because the conditional distribution corrections are being made with the aid of pseudo labels.

span.label: No single repository exists for the surveyed solutions, so the software behind the literature is scattered - the paper asks for one
span.quote: A single open-source software repository for published transfer learning solutions would be a great asset to the research community.

span.label: heterogeneous solutions mostly assume the domain distributions are the SAME, and need further adaptation steps when they are not
span.quote: The majority of the heterogeneous transfer learning solutions are focused on aligning the input spaces of the source and target domains with the assumption that the domain distributions are the same.

span.label: transferring on a defined relationship between domains is named as the least used of the four categories
span.quote: The last transfer category (and the least used approach) is to transfer knowledge based on some defined relationship between the source and target domains (examples in Mihalkova [74] and Li [62]).

span.label: transfer learning
span.quote: Therefore, there is a need to create high-performance learners trained with more easily obtained data from different domains. This methodology is referred to as transfer learning.

span.label: domain adaptation
span.quote: Domain adaptation, as it pertains to transfer learning, is the process of adapting one or more source domains for the means of transferring information to improve the performance of a target learner.

span.label: negative transfer
span.quote: negative transfer occurs when the performance of fT1(·) is greater than the performance of fT2(·). The topic of negative transfer addresses the need to quantify the amount of relatedness between the source domain and the target domain and whether an attempt to transfer knowledge from the source domain should be made.

span.label: positive transfer
span.quote: Extending the definition above, positive transfer occurs when the performance of fT2(·) is greater than the performance of fT1(·).

span.label: feature space
span.quote: A domain D is defined by two parts, a feature space X and a marginal probability distribution P(X)

span.label: domain D
span.quote: A domain D is defined by two parts, a feature space X and a marginal probability distribution P(X)

span.label: task T
span.quote: For a given domain D, a task T is defined by two parts, a label space Y, and a predictive function f(·), which is learned from the feature vector and label pairs

span.label: label space
span.quote: For a given domain D, a task T is defined by two parts, a label space Y, and a predictive function f(·), which is learned from the feature vector and label pairs

span.label: predictive function
span.quote: For a given domain D, a task T is defined by two parts, a label space Y, and a predictive function f(·), which is learned from the feature vector and label pairs

span.label: supervised transfer learning
span.quote: For example, Daumé [22] and Chattopadhyay [14] define supervised transfer learning as the case of having abundant labeled source data and limited labeled target data, and semi-supervised transfer learning as the case of abundant labeled source data and no labeled target data.

span.label: semi-supervised transfer learning
span.quote: For example, Daumé [22] and Chattopadhyay [14] define supervised transfer learning as the case of having abundant labeled source data and limited labeled target data, and semi-supervised transfer learning as the case of abundant labeled source data and no labeled target data.

span.label: inductive transfer learning
span.quote: Pan [84] refers to inductive transfer learning as the case of having available labeled target domain data, transductive transfer learning as the case of having labeled source and no labeled target domain data, and unsupervised transfer learning as the case of having no labeled source and no labeled target domain data.

span.label: transductive transfer learning
span.quote: Pan [84] refers to inductive transfer learning as the case of having available labeled target domain data, transductive transfer learning as the case of having labeled source and no labeled target domain data, and unsupervised transfer learning as the case of having no labeled source and no labeled target domain data.

span.label: unsupervised transfer learning
span.quote: Pan [84] refers to inductive transfer learning as the case of having available labeled target domain data, transductive transfer learning as the case of having labeled source and no labeled target domain data, and unsupervised transfer learning as the case of having no labeled source and no labeled target domain data.

span.label: terminology inconsistencies
span.quote: Throughout the literature on transfer learning, there are a number of terminology inconsistencies. Phrases such as transfer learning and domain adaptation are used to refer to similar processes. The following definitions will be used in this paper.

span.label: pseudo labels
span.quote: To address the lack of labeled target data, some solutions estimate the labels for the target data (called pseudo labels), which are then used to correct the conditional distribution differences. This method is problematic because the conditional distribution corrections are being made with the aid of pseudo labels.

span.label: marginal distribution
span.quote: The majority of the homogeneous transfer learning solutions employ one of three general strategies which include trying to correct for the marginal distribution difference in the source, trying to correct for the conditional distribution difference in the source, or trying to correct both the marginal and conditional distribution differences in the source.

span.label: conditional distribution
span.quote: The majority of the homogeneous transfer learning solutions employ one of three general strategies which include trying to correct for the marginal distribution difference in the source, trying to correct for the conditional distribution difference in the source, or trying to correct both the marginal and conditional distribution differences in the source.

span.label: source domain
span.quote: negative transfer occurs when the performance of fT1(·) is greater than the performance of fT2(·). The topic of negative transfer addresses the need to quantify the amount of relatedness between the source domain and the target domain and whether an attempt to transfer knowledge from the source domain should be made.

span.label: target domain
span.quote: Domain adaptation, as it pertains to transfer learning, is the process of adapting one or more source domains for the means of transferring information to improve the performance of a target learner.

span.label: context feature bias
span.quote: In a transfer learning environment, there are scenarios where a feature in the source domain may have a different meaning in the target domain.

span.label: Transfer Categories
span.quote: The form of information transfer is categorized into four general Transfer Categories [84].

span.label: asymmetric feature transformation
span.quote: The first approach transforms the features of the source through reweighting to more closely match the target domain (e.g. Pan [82]).

span.label: symmetric feature transformation
span.quote: The second approach discovers underlying meaningful structures between the domains to find a common latent feature space that has predictive qualities while reducing the marginal distribution between the domains (e.g. Blitzer [5]).

span.label: feature augmentation method
span.quote: To resolve context feature bias, a method to augment the source and target feature space with three duplicate copies of the original feature set is proposed.

span.label: informed supervised transfer learning
span.quote: Cook [19] and Feuz [36] provide a different variation where the definition of supervised or unsupervised refers to the presence or absence of labeled data in the source domain and informed or uninformed refers to the presence or absence of labeled data in the target domain. With this definition, a labeled source and limited labeled target domain is referred to as informed supervised transfer learning

span.label: transductive transfer learning
span.quote: Pan [84] refers to inductive transfer learning as the case of having available labeled target domain data, transductive transfer learning as the case of having labeled source and no labeled target domain data, and unsupervised transfer learning as the case of having no labeled source and no labeled target domain data

span.label: supervised transfer learning - DAUME AND CHATTOPADHYAY'S SENSE: abundant labeled source data and LIMITED labeled target data
span.quote: For example, Daumé [22] and Chattopadhyay [14] define supervised transfer learning as the case of having abundant labeled source data and limited labeled target data, and semi-supervised transfer learning as the case of abundant labeled source data and no labeled target data.

span.label: semi-supervised transfer learning - DAUME AND CHATTOPADHYAY'S SENSE: abundant labeled source and NO labeled target. Gong and Blitzer use this same phrase for what Daume calls SUPERVISED - the two labels are swapped between literatures
span.quote: For example, Daumé [22] and Chattopadhyay [14] define supervised transfer learning as the case of having abundant labeled source data and limited labeled target data, and semi-supervised transfer learning as the case of abundant labeled source data and no labeled target data.

span.label: unsupervised transfer learning - PAN'S SENSE: NO labeled source and NO labeled target, where the same phrase elsewhere in the literature means abundant labeled source and no labeled target. THREE GROUPS, ONE VOCABULARY, THREE MAPPINGS
span.quote: Pan [84] refers to inductive transfer learning as the case of having available labeled target domain data, transductive transfer learning as the case of having labeled source and no labeled target domain data, and unsupervised transfer learning as the case of having no labeled source and no labeled target domain data.

span.label: transfer learning - the paper's response to its own finding: it refuses the contested labels entirely and states the data conditions each time instead of naming them
span.quote: This paper will explicitly state when labeled and unlabeled data are being used in the source and target domains.

span.label: `supervised transfer learning` - DAUME AND CHATTOPADHYAY'S SENSE: `abundant labeled source data and LIMITED labeled target data`. Gong and Blitzer give that same configuration to SEMI-SUPERVISED, and Cook and Feuz call it INFORMED SUPERVISED.
span.quote: For example, Daumé [22] and Chattopadhyay [14] define supervised transfer learning as the case of having abundant labeled source data and limited labeled target data, and semi-supervised transfer learning as the case of abundant labeled source data and no labeled target data

span.label: `semi-supervised transfer learning` - GONG AND BLITZER'S SENSE: `abundant labeled source data and LIMITED labeled target data`. THAT IS THE CONFIGURATION Daume and Chattopadhyay CALL SUPERVISED - see senses[4] and the `daume` mechanism on this record, which quote their sentence. One name over two configurations and one configuration under two names, in consecutive sentences.
span.quote: In Gong [42] and Blitzer [5], semi-supervised transfer learning is the case of having abundant labeled source data and limited labeled target data

span.label: `supervised` / `unsupervised` - COOK AND FEUZ MOVE THE AXIS: the pair refers to `the presence or absence of labeled data IN THE SOURCE domain` and a SECOND pair, `informed` / `uninformed`, carries the target. Two orthogonal axes where the other schemes have one.
span.quote: Cook [19] and Feuz [36] provide a different variation where the definition of supervised or unsupervised refers to the presence or absence of labeled data in the source domain and informed or uninformed refers to the presence or absence of labeled data in the target domain. With this definition, a labeled source and limited labeled target domain is referred to as informed supervised transfer learning

span.label: `domain adaptation` - AS STIPULATED HERE, because the field does not agree: `the process of ADAPTING ONE OR MORE SOURCE DOMAINS for the means of transferring information to improve the performance of a target learner`, by bringing the source's distribution closer to the target's.
span.quote: Domain adaptation, as it pertains to transfer learning, is the process of adapting one or more source domains for the means of transferring information to improve the performance of a target learner. The domain adaptation process attempts to alter a source domain in an attempt to bring the distribution of the source closer to that of the target

span.label: domain adaptation —part-of→ transfer learning
span.quote: Domain adaptation, as it pertains to transfer learning, is the process of adapting one or more source domains for the means of transferring information to improve the performance of a target learner.

span.label: negative transfer —distinct-from→ positive transfer
span.quote: Extending the definition above, positive transfer occurs when the performance of fT2(·) is greater than the performance of fT1(·).

span.label: feature space —part-of→ domain D
span.quote: A domain D is defined by two parts, a feature space X and a marginal probability distribution P(X)

span.label: label space —part-of→ task T
span.quote: For a given domain D, a task T is defined by two parts, a label space Y, and a predictive function f(·), which is learned from the feature vector and label pairs

span.label: predictive function —part-of→ task T
span.quote: For a given domain D, a task T is defined by two parts, a label space Y, and a predictive function f(·), which is learned from the feature vector and label pairs

span.label: in the muscle-fatigue test EVERY transfer learning approach beat the non-transfer baseline, with the two proposed methods ranking first and second
span.quote: The order of performance from best to worst is 2SW-MDA, CP-MDA, Duan [29], Zhong [143], Gao [37], Pan [87], Huang [51], and the baseline approach.

span.label: an often-cited domain adaptation method is reported as requiring only ten lines of Perl - the simplicity is the claim
span.quote: In an early and often cited work, Daumé [22] proposes a simple domain adaptation algorithm, referred to as the feature augmentation method (FAM), requiring only ten lines of Perl script that uses labeled source data and limited labeled target data.

span.label: homogeneous transfer learning is presented as directly applicable to big data because it lets an existing related dataset stand in for costly new collection
span.quote: The methodology of homogeneous transfer learning is directly applicable to a big data environment.

span.label: the four transfer categories enumerated by what is carried across
span.quote: The form of information transfer is categorized into four general Transfer Categories [84].

span.label: context feature bias defined by its consequence - it makes the conditional distributions differ
span.quote: The issue is referred to as context feature bias, which causes the conditional distributions between the source and target domains to be different.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1186/s40537-016-0043-6.
